domain: Islamic Jurisprudence / Legal Hermeneutics / Gender Studies
topic_summary: Analysis of specific Qur'anic verses establishing inheritance ratios, testimony weight, and family roles as a contested canonical kernel. Two structurally incompatible readings: literal-hierarchical (verses as timeless legal constraints fixing male guardianship) versus contextual-egalitarian (verses as historically situated, requiring reinterpretation under overarching equity principles). Authority structures differ fundamentally—classical fiqh consensus versus maqasid hermeneutics—producing constraints with opposite beneficiary/victim structures.

key_entities: Classical fiqh schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali juristic tradition)
Male household heads (beneficiaries under hierarchical reading)
Women and gender minorities (victims under hierarchical reading, beneficiaries under egalitarian reading)
Religious courts (qadi courts, sharia councils enforcing interpretations)
Rights-based NGOs (structural advocates for gender equity)
key_tensions: Literal textualism vs contextual hermeneutics (interpretive authority contest)
Male guardianship security vs women's legal autonomy (resource and authority control)
key_claims: Inheritance verse 4:11 establishes 2:1 male-female ratio as divine legal prescription
Testimony verse 2:282 requires two female witnesses to equal one male witness
Guardianship verse 4:34 establishes qiwamah (male authority over women) as structural household norm
Maqasid framework allows reinterpretation when literal application contradicts overarching justice principles
key_mechanisms: Ijma' (juristic consensus) stabilizes traditional interpretations across madhahib
Tafsir (exegetical tradition) transmits and reinforces literal-hierarchical readings
Ijtihad (independent reasoning) enables contextual reinterpretation when deployed by reformists
key_absences: Queer and trans jurisprudence—gender binary is uncontested substrate in both readings
Economic context dependency—verse 4:11's inheritance ratio assumes male financial obligation (nafaqah) which may not hold in contemporary dual-income households

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Specific Qur'anic verses (4:11 inheritance, 2:282 testimony, 4:34 guardianship) as fixed canonical text establishing gender-differentiated legal and family roles
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Interpretive legitimacy contested: classical fiqh grounds authority in ijma' and transmitted tafsir; maqasid hermeneutics grounds authority in overarching Qur'anic objectives (justice, equity, human dignity) permitting contextual reinterpretation
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Stabilization / Interpretive Ambiguity Hybrid—kernel text is fixed and unambiguous in literal reading, but maqasid framework treats literalism itself as a layer absorbing historical drift, with reform proposed as return to true underlying objectives rather than revision

readings.commitment: Verses 4:11, 2:282, 4:34 are direct, timeless legal constraints establishing male guardianship and differentiated rights as divine ordinance
readings.authority_grounding: Classical fiqh ijma' (juristic consensus across madhahib); transmitted tafsir tradition; textualist usul al-fiqh
readings.expected_structural_delta: High base extractiveness—male household heads and religious courts gain structural authority and resource control; women enter victim set with constrained inheritance, testimony weight, and legal autonomy; exit costs high (apostasy/family rupture)

readings.commitment: Same verses are historically situated progressive steps within 7th-century Arabia, requiring reinterpretation under overarching Qur'anic equity principles (maqasid)
readings.authority_grounding: Maqasid al-Shari'ah framework; reformist ijtihad; appeal to Qur'anic meta-principles (justice, dignity, no compulsion)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Moderate extractiveness—reformist scholars and rights-based NGOs gain interpretive authority; women exit victim set and gain structural claims to equal inheritance/testimony; patriarchal elites and traditional courts lose discretionary power; intra-community conflict over legitimacy

readings.commitment: Verses represent an incomplete trajectory—later egalitarian principles in Qur'an (e.g., 49:13 universal human dignity) supersede earlier gender-specific rules via principle of naskh (abrogation)
readings.authority_grounding: Selective application of classical naskh doctrine; progressive theological movements; secular feminist frameworks imported into Islamic discourse
readings.expected_structural_delta: Very high extractiveness—complete normative reversal; traditional authority structures comprehensively delegitimized; women gain full legal parity; risk of epistemic violence against communities whose identity is bound to literal reading; high exit costs for scholars adopting this reading within traditional institutions

axiom_contradictions.basis: Accepting that divine legal prescription can be contextually reinterpreted requires rejecting the axiom that explicit Qur'anic legal rulings are timeless and directly applicable—no single framework can hold both 'the 2:1 inheritance ratio is immutable divine law' and 'the 2:1 ratio was a historically bounded step toward equity that maqasid now supersedes'

Accepting that later egalitarian verses abrogate earlier gender-specific rules requires rejecting the axiom that all explicit legal rulings remain in force unless explicitly abrogated by another explicit ruling—classical naskh doctrine does not permit principle-based abrogation of clear legal verse

Contextual reading treats verses as valid but requiring reinterpretation; abrogation reading treats verses as superseded/invalid—no single framework can hold both 'verse 4:11 remains valid when properly contextualized' and 'verse 4:11 is abrogated by verse 49:13'

axes.human_readable: Literal-Hierarchical Reading (Verses as Timeless Legal Constraints)
axes.structural_delta: Qur'anic gender verses read as direct, immutable divine legal prescriptions establishing male guardianship and differentiated inheritance/testimony rights
axes.primary_observable: Fiqh rulings in inheritance cases (2:1 ratio enforcement); testimony admissibility rules in Islamic courts; prevalence of male qiwamah invocation in family disputes
axes.selection_reason: Core reading with highest structural extractiveness and clearest beneficiary/victim structure; establishes baseline constraint from which other readings diverge

axes.human_readable: Contextual-Egalitarian Reading (Verses as Historically Situated Steps)
axes.structural_delta: Same Qur'anic verses reinterpreted as 7th-century progressive reforms requiring further evolution under overarching equity principles (maqasid)
axes.primary_observable: Adoption of maqasid hermeneutics in reformist institutions; legal reforms allowing equal inheritance in Muslim-majority states; fatwas citing contextual interpretation
axes.selection_reason: Structurally distinct reading with opposite beneficiary/victim mapping; moderate extractiveness due to intra-community legitimacy contest

axes.human_readable: Progressive Abrogation Reading (Later Egalitarian Principles Supersede Gender-Specific Rules)
axes.structural_delta: Gender-specific verses treated as superseded by later universalist principles via reinterpretation of naskh doctrine
axes.primary_observable: Theological movements citing verse 49:13 to override 4:11; secular-Islamic feminist discourse; legal systems fully equalizing gender rights in Muslim-majority contexts
axes.selection_reason: Highest extractiveness reading; represents maximal structural divergence from literal reading; captures epistemic violence dimension absent in contextual reading

axes.human_readable: Economic Context Dependency (Inheritance Ratio Assumed Male Financial Obligation)
axes.structural_delta: Verse 4:11's 2:1 inheritance ratio presumes male nafaqah (financial maintenance obligation) which may not hold in dual-income households
axes.primary_observable: Female labor force participation rates in Muslim-majority countries; household income distribution data; legal enforcement of nafaqah vs actual practice
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: structural support for contextual reading but lower independent yield than three selected readings; economic substrate is rope (coordination problem) rather than tangled_rope

axes.human_readable: Queer/Trans Jurisprudence Erasure (Gender Binary as Uncontested Substrate)
axes.structural_delta: Both literal and contextual readings assume binary gender framework, erasing non-binary and transgender jurisprudential questions
axes.primary_observable: Absence of trans-inclusive inheritance/testimony rulings; lack of non-binary gender categories in Islamic legal discourse; activist pressure from LGBTQ+ Muslim organizations
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: critical absence but outside the literal-contextual kernel contest; would require separate generative axis as all three readings share this blind spot; flagged for omega treatment

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Inheritance ratio presumes male financial obligation obsolete in dual-income contexts
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Structural support for contextual reading but lower yield than three selected readings; economic substrate coordination problem captured implicitly in contextual reading's beneficiary structure

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Gender binary assumed by all readings, erasing non-binary and transgender jurisprudence
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Critical structural absence but outside kernel contest topology—all three readings share this blind spot; requires independent generative treatment rather than integration into current kernel decomposition; omega variable

omegas.description: All three readings (literal, contextual, abrogation) assume binary gender framework. What constraint structure emerges when non-binary and transgender Muslims demand inheritance/testimony recognition? Is the gender binary itself a Mountain (biological essentialism claimed), Rope (social coordination), or Piton (constructed via interpretive tradition)? Current kernel decomposition cannot address this—deferred axis queer_trans_erasure would require separate generation pass with independent reading structure.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) + deferred axis queer_trans_erasure

omegas.description: Constraint extractiveness varies radically with state enforcement. In states with compulsory Islamic inheritance (e.g., Saudi, Iran pre-reform), literal reading operates as enforced Snare; in states with opt-in sharia courts (e.g., UK, India), it operates as Scaffold (voluntary community norm). This topology shift is not captured in reading-level analysis—may require state-enforcement axis in expanded treatment.

Shia jurisprudence (particularly Ja'fari school) has different inheritance rules for daughters in absence of sons—does this constitute a fourth reading, or is it a separate kernel? Sunni-Shia split may multiply kernel count rather than reading count within single kernel.
omegas.source: F15 (Premature Closure) check—stopped at three Sunni-dominant readings

omegas.description: Progressive abrogation reading's use of naskh doctrine is contested—classical naskh requires explicit textual abrogation, not principle-based supersession. Is this reading an internal Islamic hermeneutic or an external feminist framework imported with Islamic vocabulary? Epistemic trespass risk if progressive_abrogation is not recognized as legitimate Islamic discourse by substantial scholarly consensus.
omegas.source: F34 (Epistemic Trespass) consideration + axiom_contradiction between contextual and abrogation readings
